subject: economics
title: ZIMSEC A-Level Economics

officialDocument.title: Economics Syllabus, Forms 5 - 6, 2015 - 2022 (Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education, Curriculum Development and Technical Services), examined by ZIMSEC at A Level
officialDocument.publisher: Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education (Curriculum Development and Technical Services) / Zimbabwe School Examinations Council (ZIMSEC)

sourceNote: Topic names and their order (1 to 11) are transcribed from the topic list (6.0) of the Ministry's Economics Syllabus Forms 5 - 6 (2015 - 2022). Sub-topics are the key concepts of the competency matrix (8.0), which prints them without numbers, so all sub-topic codes (1.1 ...), all objective codes and the Examination skills node S are ours; the form in which each is taught comes from the matrix (8.1 Form 5, 8.2 Form 6) and the scope and sequence (7.0). Learning-objective statements are our own paraphrase; no syllabus text is reproduced.
notes: Source (read 2026-10-08): Ministry document, copy obtained from zimsake.co.zw softidrive (the zimsake.co.zw document library; the URL recorded is the library's https address because the file has no stable direct link). The cover prints 'Economics Syllabus Forms 5 - 6, 2015 - 2022' (Curriculum Development and Technical Services, Harare, 2015). It was read through a pdftotext rendering in which the scope-and-sequence and competency-matrix tables come out with their columns interleaved, and parts of the assessment pages (the description of papers and a pie chart) are overprinted; check every heading, the form of each item and each objective against a clean copy from ZIMSEC.
Subject code: not printed in the document and not verified by us; code left null. Confirm the examination code with ZIMSEC.

Heritage-Based Curriculum: ZIMSEC introduced Heritage-Based Curriculum syllabi for Forms 5-6, and newer versions exist for some subjects. The version of Economics that November 2026 and later A-Level candidates sit must be confirmed; set effectiveTo and add a new version file when a new syllabus replaces this one. Version dates assumed: first examined in November 2018 (effectiveFrom 2018-01-01).

Numbering: the topic list numbers the eleven topics 6.1-6.11, the scope and sequence 7.1-7.11, and the competency matrix numbers them by form (Form 5: 8.1.1-8.1.11; Form 6: 8.2.1-8.2.9, which has no Tools of Economic Analysis or Economic Resources topic and starts with Demand Theory). This tree follows the topic list (1-11) and puts each key concept under its topic with the form that teaches it. Interest rate determination appears in the matrix under both Theory of Distribution (8.2.4) and Money and the Price Level (8.2.8); it is transcribed once, at 10.5.

Gaps and doubts in the copy read: the headers and footers of the assessment pages say 'Economics Syllabus Forms 1 - 4' (a copy-and-paste slip in the document). Form 6 key concepts have no objectives for some scope-and-sequence items (comparison and evaluation of market structures, advantages and disadvantages of each market structure, application to an economy); they are attached to 5.3 and 5.5. The multiplier, the accelerator and the Phillips curve appear in the checklist of terms (10.0) but not in the matrix; they are covered at 9.5, 11.4 and the lesson on consumption, saving and investment. The checklist also names point elasticity, Marshall-Lerner, the J-curve, cartels, natural monopoly, purchasing power parity and the quantity theory of money. Cambridge-style game theory (Prisoner's Dilemma) is not printed in the ZIMSEC copy; the collusion lesson covers cartels for ZIMSEC and game theory for Cambridge.

Assessment (9.0) as read: continuous assessment 30% (Form 5 10%, Form 6 20%: an assignment and a theory test per term and a practical assignment per year) and a summative examination 70%: Paper 1 multiple choice (40 items with four options, 1 hour 30 minutes, 40 marks, 20%), Paper 2 data response (two compulsory questions of 20 marks each, 1 hour 15 minutes, 40 marks, 20%) and Paper 3 theory essays (12 questions, candidates answer 4, 3 hours, 100 marks, 30%). The pie chart on the same page appears to show 25% for Paper 3; the table and the description both say 30%, which is what is recorded. Papers 1 and 2 list all eleven topics; Paper 3 lists ten (Tools of Economic Analysis is not examined in Paper 3). Skill distribution as printed: Paper 1 knowledge and understanding 20-25%, interpretation and application 50-55%, analysis 20-25%; Paper 2 knowledge 20%, interpretation and application 40%, analysis 30%, organisation, presentation and communication 10%; Paper 3 knowledge 28%, interpretation and application 16%, analysis 20%, evaluation 36%.

Marks per essay: the document gives 100 marks for four answered questions, so we assume 25 marks per essay; whether the essays have parts is not stated (our practice convention uses (a) and (b)). The part structure of Paper 2 is not stated either. A reviewer must check both against recent papers. Continuous assessment (Paper 4) is not a component here and is not simulated.

Many concepts are shared with Cambridge 9708 (concepts aecon.*). Lessons are written to the depth of the deeper board; parts named only by ZIMSEC (data collection and presentation, business organisation and ethics, sources of capital, small and medium enterprises, wages legislation, land reform, the Zimbabwean decision-making process, schools of thought, commodity agreements, the Look East policy) are marked as ZIMSEC detail. Zimbabwean content is factual and politically neutral, and every data set is illustrative.
overview: The ZIMSEC A-Level Economics syllabus (Forms 5-6) has eleven topics. Form 5 covers the tools of economic analysis (research techniques, averages and data presentation), economic resources, enterprise and business organisation, demand, supply and elasticity, production costs, the theory of the firm and market structures, rewards to the factors of production, market failure and government intervention, international trade, national income measurement, money and banking and macroeconomic problems. Form 6 adds utility and indifference curve theory, growth of firms and small enterprises, profits, efficiency and price discrimination, theories of distribution, cost-benefit analysis and central planning, the balance of payments, terms of trade and exchange rates, national income determination and aggregate demand and supply, interest rates and inflation, and macroeconomic objectives and policies, with emphasis on Zimbabwe.
assessmentOverview: Continuous assessment (assignments, theory tests and a practical assignment) carries 30%. The examination carries 70%: Paper 1 multiple choice (40 items, 1 hour 30 minutes, 20%), Paper 2 data response (two compulsory questions of 20 marks, 1 hour 15 minutes, 20%) and Paper 3 theory essays (12 questions, answer 4, 3 hours, 100 marks, 30%).

components.name: Paper 1: Multiple choice
components.description: 40 compulsory four-option multiple-choice items on all eleven topics.

components.name: Paper 2: Data response
components.description: Two compulsory data-response questions of 20 marks each, testing knowledge, understanding and problem solving, on all eleven topics.

components.name: Paper 3: Theory essays
components.description: Twelve essay questions; candidates answer four (100 marks, so about 25 each). Topics 2-11 (Tools of Economic Analysis is not listed for this paper).

topics.name: Tools of Economic Analysis
topics.description: Form 5 (competency matrix 8.1.1). Not listed among the topics of Paper 3.

objectives.text: Explain the methods of collecting economic data: interviews, questionnaires, surveys, observation, sampling and experiments.
Compare and contrast the methods and state the strengths and weaknesses of each.
Draft a short questionnaire for a simple economic enquiry.

children.name: Measures of central tendency, and presentation and analysis of economic data
children.description: The matrix lists 'Measures of central tendency' and 'Presentation and analysis of economic data' as two key concepts; they are taught together in one lesson and transcribed as one node.

objectives.text: Calculate the mean, mode and median.
Compile data from a schedule and present it in pie charts, bar charts, frequency polygons, line graphs, tables and pictorial form.
Interpret and compare economic data given in graphical, pictorial and numerical form.
Explain the factors of production (land, labour, capital, enterprise) and distinguish renewable from non-renewable resources.
Analyse the relationship between wants and available resources (scarcity), and explain choice and opportunity cost.
Use production possibility curves to show scarcity, choice, opportunity cost and efficiency.
Illustrate efficiency, inefficiency and unattainable points, and explain increasing, decreasing and constant opportunity cost and the different shapes of the curve.

children.name: Economic systems and the role of price

objectives.text: Compare resource allocation in market, planned and mixed economies and analyse the Zimbabwean system.
Discuss the role of price in signalling, rationing and rewarding.
Explain the characteristics of a successful entrepreneur (risk-taking, using opportunities).
Assess the requirements for business formation: idea generation, a business proposal, licensing and registration.
Explain sources of capital (loans, shares, leasing, hire purchase, personal savings) and analyse the procedures for acquiring capital.

children.name: Business organisations and business ethics
children.description: The matrix lists 'Business organisations' and 'Business ethics' as two key concepts; transcribed as one node because one lesson covers both.

objectives.text: Examine and select the type of business organisation (sole trader, partnership, cooperative, private and public limited company) suited to one's environment.
Explain business ethics: Unhu/Ubuntu/Vumunhu, accountability, social responsibility and environmental consciousness.

topics.name: Demand Theory
topics.description: Form 5 (competency matrix 8.1.3: demand and elasticity) and Form 6 (8.2.1: utility and indifference curve theories).

objectives.text: Analyse the causes of movements along the demand curve and shifts of the demand curve, for individuals and the market.
Explain and calculate price, income and cross elasticities of demand and interpret the numerical values.
Explain the factors affecting elasticity of demand.
Evaluate the importance of elasticity for households, firms and government, including its implications for revenue.
Explain diminishing marginal utility and the equi-marginal principle, and examine the limitations of marginal utility theory.
Distinguish normal from inferior goods using the substitution and income effects of a price change, with indifference curve analysis.

topics.name: Supply Theory
topics.description: Form 5 (competency matrix 8.1.4) and Form 6 (8.2.2: growth of firms and small and medium enterprises).

objectives.text: Explain the determinants of supply and distinguish movements along from shifts of the supply curve, for individuals and the market.

children.name: Equilibrium price and quantity, consumer and producer surplus

objectives.text: Explain how equilibrium price and quantity are established and show the effects of shifts of demand and supply.
Distinguish between consumer surplus and producer surplus.
Calculate price elasticity of supply, analyse its determinants and evaluate its importance.
Explain the short run and the long run and calculate total, marginal and average costs.
Distinguish between internal and external economies and diseconomies of scale.
Explain the reasons for the growth of firms and analyse the methods of growth: integration, mergers and diversification.
Assess the benefits and costs of large firms, including multinational firms, to the economy.

children.name: Survival of small and medium enterprises

objectives.text: Justify the survival of small and medium enterprises and evaluate their benefits.
Analyse the reasons for government involvement in the creation of small and medium enterprises.
Explain the objectives of firms: profit maximisation, survival, growth and sales maximisation.
Describe the equilibrium conditions of the firm (such as MC = MR) and apply demand and supply analysis to its price and output.
Explain the concept of market structure and the features of perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and contestable markets.
Analyse the factors that influence the pricing and output decisions of firms in each structure.
Compare and contrast market structures.
Explain normal and abnormal profits, losses, cost minimisation and profit maximisation.
Assess allocative, productive and technical efficiency, and evaluate the efficiency of firms in different market structures.
Explain price discrimination and analyse the conditions for it and its effects.

topics.name: Theory of Distribution
topics.description: Form 5 (competency matrix 8.1.6) and Form 6 (8.2.4). The matrix also lists interest rate determination (Loanable Funds and Liquidity Preference theories) here and under Money and the Price Level; it is transcribed once, as 10.5.

objectives.text: Explain the rewards to the factors of production: rent, wages, interest and profit.
Distinguish between economic rent, quasi-rent and transfer earnings.

children.name: Determination of rewards: marginal revenue productivity and demand and supply

objectives.text: Apply the Marginal Revenue Productivity Theory to the demand for land, capital and labour.
Explain the determination of rewards using the theory of demand and supply of factors of production.
Analyse imperfections in the labour market and apply the theories to an economy such as Zimbabwe.
Explain wage differentials and justify their existence using economic and non-economic theories.
Explain the reasons for government intervention: public goods, externalities, market imperfections, merit and demerit goods and common property.
Identify market failure in the learner's own environment.
Explain how taxation and subsidies are used to correct market failure.

children.name: Price controls, production quotas and buffer stock

objectives.text: Explain price controls and buffer stock schemes as methods of government intervention.
Explain direct provision, regulation and quotas as methods of government intervention.
Explain privatisation, commercialisation and nationalisation as methods of intervention.

children.name: Wages legislation, incomes policy and land reform

objectives.text: Explain wages legislation, incomes policy, controls on trade unions and the land reform programme as interventions, and suggest solutions to market failure in the community.

children.name: Strengths and weaknesses of solutions to market failure

objectives.text: Analyse the effectiveness of government intervention in an economy such as Zimbabwe, with the strengths and weaknesses of each solution.

children.name: Central planning and decision-making in Zimbabwe

objectives.text: Assess the effectiveness (strengths and weaknesses) of central planning in an economy.
Analyse the decision-making process in Zimbabwe.
Analyse the applicability of cost-benefit analysis as a decision-making tool.
Explain absolute and comparative advantage and the reasons for trade, including Zimbabwe's position.

children.name: Free trade and the determinants of trade flows

objectives.text: Explain the determinants of trade flows, including political factors, and justify free trade by weighing the arguments for and against it.
Explain and evaluate the types of protectionism, such as tariffs and quotas.
Explain economic integration (free trade area, customs union, economic union) and assess the merits and demerits of each.
Examine commodity agreements (including GATT and bilateral agreements).
Examine the components of the balance of payments: current account, capital account and balance for official financing.
Calculate balance of payments figures and assess surplus and deficit.

children.name: Balance of payments disequilibrium and trade policies

objectives.text: Evaluate policy measures to correct disequilibrium: exchange rate policy, import substitution, protectionism, export promotion and the Look East policy.
Calculate the terms of trade from export and import price indices and interpret them.

children.name: Exchange rates and exchange rate regimes

objectives.text: Assess the operation of exchange rates and of fixed, floating and managed regimes.
Explain the flow of national income in closed and open economies.
Calculate national income using the output, income and expenditure approaches (GDP, GNP, NNP, per capita income).
Compare national income statistics between countries and within the same country, and assess their usefulness.

children.name: GDP deflator, nominal and real income

objectives.text: Distinguish nominal from real income and calculate real income using the GDP deflator.
Compare living standards between countries and over time.
Explain national income determination from consumption, investment, government expenditure and net exports, and illustrate equilibrium national income.
Explain inflationary and deflationary gaps.
Discuss the main schools of thought: Keynesians and monetarists.
Analyse the components of aggregate demand and aggregate supply and their interaction.
Explain the characteristics of money and examine its functions.
Explain the functions and role of the central bank, commercial banks, building societies and merchant banks in an economy.
Illustrate how banks create money and calculate the money multiplier.
Discuss the impact of credit creation in an economy.
Explain the determinants of the demand for and the supply of money.

children.name: Interest rate determination
children.description: Also listed in the matrix under Theory of Distribution (8.2.4).

objectives.text: Examine and evaluate the Loanable Funds and Liquidity Preference theories, and non-economic determinants, in explaining interest rates in an economy.

children.name: Inflation
children.description: Includes the Consumer Price Index and Retail Price Index (measurement is taught in the lesson covered at 9.3).

objectives.text: Explain how inflation is measured (CPI and RPI) and the relationship between the money supply and the price level (Quantity Theory of Money).
Discuss the causes and effects of inflation and the effectiveness of measures used to control it.

children.name: Macroeconomic problems
children.description: The matrix names unemployment, inflation, balance of payments and exchange rates as the problems; inflation, the balance of payments and exchange rates are covered at 10.6, 8.5-8.6 and 8.8.

objectives.text: Analyse the causes of macroeconomic problems such as unemployment and assess their effects.

children.name: Characteristics of developing and developed countries

objectives.text: Distinguish between developing and developed economies by their characteristics.
Explain the macroeconomic objectives: price stability, full employment, economic growth and development, and equity.
Examine the relationship among macroeconomic objectives, such as the trade-off between price stability and unemployment.

children.name: Macroeconomic policies: fiscal, monetary and exchange rate

objectives.text: Analyse fiscal policy, monetary policy and exchange rate policy and their effects.

children.name: Evaluating policies and conflicting policy objectives

objectives.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of macroeconomic policies, with emphasis on the Zimbabwean economy, and the conflicts among policy objectives.

topics.name: Examination skills
topics.description: Not a content topic of the syllabus: this node is ours, from the assessment objectives and the skill distribution (knowledge and understanding, interpretation and application, analysis, evaluation, organisation and communication).

children.name: Data response: diagrams, data and calculations

objectives.text: Interpret and comment on economic phenomena presented in scenarios, tables and graphs.
Apply theory and calculations to data to solve economic problems.
Organise, present and communicate economic ideas and make informed judgements in a clear, logical and appropriate form.
Analyse and evaluate arguments, proposals and policies in the light of economic theory and social values.
